stories.headline: OIL SURGES TO SIX-WEEK HIGHS AS US STRIKES ON IRAN ENTER AN 11TH NIGHT AND HOUTHIS THREATEN A SAUDI BLOCKADE
stories.body: WTI jumped to roughly $87 a barrel (+3.0%) and Brent rose to about $94 (+3.4%), both six-week highs, after US Central Command carried out its 11th consecutive night of strikes on Iran and Iran-aligned Houthi rebels threatened to blockade Saudi Arabia and restrict tanker traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The S&P 500 slipped only 0.14% and the Nasdaq 100 fell about 0.5%, suggesting equities still see the disruption as commodity-specific rather than a broader growth threat.
stories.explain: Oil's jump reflects a rising war-risk premium priced into the physical barrel - traders bidding up crude on the probability that supply gets disrupted at a chokepoint, not on any change in actual production yet. Bab el-Mandeb carries a meaningful share of global seaborne oil traffic bound for Europe, so a credible blockade threat forces tankers to reroute around Africa's Cape of Good Hope, adding weeks of transit time and cost that show up as a price premium long before a single barrel actually goes missing. Equities' muted reaction versus oil's 3% pop tells you traders still see this as a supply-side commodity story rather than a system-wide risk-off event - a read that would break fast if Hormuz itself got blocked, since roughly a fifth of global oil transits there daily.

stories.headline: STOCKS SLIP AS ALPHABET'S CAPEX WORRIES OVERSHADOW ANOTHER MEMORY-CHIP RALLY
stories.body: The S&P 500 eased 0.14% to 7,498.96 and the Nasdaq 100 fell roughly 0.5% as Alphabet shares dropped after-hours despite beating Q2 estimates, on investor concern over ballooning AI capital spending; Tesla and IBM also reported. Even so, Micron (+210% YTD) and SanDisk (+503% YTD, the Nasdaq 100's top performer) kept climbing on Morgan Stanley's forecast that memory prices could rise more than 25% through Q3, and AMD picked up fresh price-target hikes (Rosenblatt to $665, UBS to $700) ahead of its AI conference.
stories.explain: The market is drawing a sharp line between AI capex as an expense and AI capex as a revenue driver: Alphabet's selloff despite beating earnings shows investors punishing spending they can't yet tie to a return, while Micron and SanDisk keep rallying because higher memory prices translate almost directly into their margins with no execution risk in between. That's why a soft mega-cap earnings reaction and a strong semiconductor rally are showing up in the same tape on the same day - they are pricing two different parts of the same AI buildout, the spenders versus the suppliers, and the market currently trusts the suppliers' numbers more than the spenders' promises.

stories.headline: TREASURY YIELDS TICK HIGHER AS TRADERS RAISE THE ODDS OF A JULY RATE HIKE AHEAD OF WARSH'S SECOND FOMC MEETING
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield rose about 2 basis points to 4.64% as prediction markets pushed the odds of a hike at the July 28-29 FOMC meeting to roughly 26%, with the probability climbing to about 43% by September under Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who has repeatedly said current prices are 'too high.'
stories.explain: A rate hike this cycle would be an unusual move - most of this FOMC's debate has centered on whether to cut given a cooling labor market, so a rising hike probability signals traders think Warsh's committee is now weighting sticky inflation (June's dot plot lifted the year-end PCE forecast to 3.6%) more heavily than employment risk. The 2-bp yield move looks small, but it lands the same day oil jumped 3% on Iran escalation - energy shocks feed directly into headline inflation, handing hawks a fresh data point six days before the meeting.

stories.headline: BRAZIL'S 25% TARIFF TAKES EFFECT AS PROMISED, WITH A FORCED-LABOR PROBE THREATENING TO ADD MORE
stories.body: The US's 25% Section 301 tariff on most Brazilian imports took effect Wednesday as scheduled, targeting goods tied to Brazil's Pix payment rules, deforestation policy, and content-moderation orders against US tech firms; beef, orange juice, aircraft parts, energy, and some raw materials and pharmaceuticals were carved out. A separate forced-labor investigation could layer on another 12.5% duty.
stories.explain: By exempting beef, OJ, and aircraft parts - categories where the US either has few substitute suppliers or where a domestic industry depends on the imported input - USTR is deliberately shrinking the tariff's inflation footprint on US consumers while still hitting its political targets. That carve-out strategy is why this round is reading as a trade-policy story rather than a market-moving one: the goods still covered are ones where the US has more substitute options, so more of the 25% is likely to be absorbed by Brazilian exporters cutting prices rather than passed through to American shelves.

stories.headline: GOLD PUSHES TOWARD $4,150 AS MIDEAST ESCALATION OUTWEIGHS A STEADY DOLLAR
stories.body: Gold traded up to roughly $4,135 an ounce (+1.6%) as safe-haven buying tied to the escalating Iran conflict overpowered a nearly flat US Dollar Index (101.12, -0.05%) heading into next week's Fed decision.
stories.explain: Gold pays no coupon, so its price move is a pure read on how much investors are willing to sacrifice in foregone Treasury income (currently about 4.64% on the 10-year) to hold a hedge against war risk or inflation. Today's gain despite a stable dollar shows geopolitical-hedge demand is currently doing more work than the rates or currency channels - a combination that could reverse quickly if the Fed delivers a hawkish surprise next week that pushes real yields meaningfully higher.

stories.headline: MICHIGAN'S OFFSEASON TURMOIL CONTINUES AS AD WARDE MANUEL'S STEP-DOWN STILL REVERBERATES
stories.body: Athletic director Warde Manuel's decision to step down at year-end following an independent Jenner & Block review remains the biggest storyline in men's college basketball as the sport sits in its deepest offseason lull; Manuel's staff already converted interim coach Mike Boynton Jr. into the permanent head coach on a two-year deal after national champion Dusty May left for the Dallas Mavericks' head job in late June.

stories.headline: GOLDEN STATE WINS SUMMER LEAGUE TITLE AS ROOKIE YAXEL LENDEBORG TAKES HOME MVP
stories.body: The Warriors beat the Grizzlies 94-90 in the Las Vegas Summer League championship, with rookie Yaxel Lendeborg outdueling Grizzlies rookie Cameron Boozer with 21 points, 10 rebounds, 2 assists, and 2 steals in 23 minutes to claim Summer League MVP.

stories.headline: CARDINALS GUARD ISAIAH ADAMS FACES FOUR WEAPONS CHARGES BUT REPORTS TO TRAINING CAMP
stories.body: Arizona lineman Isaiah Adams, a 2024 third-round pick who started 11 games last season, turned himself in over the weekend on four charges - including possessing a restricted firearm without a license - stemming from a Canadian 'guns and gangs' investigation, and is still expected to report to camp Wednesday as all 32 NFL teams open camp by July 28.

stories.headline: SEC MEDIA DAYS DAY THREE: OLE MISS'S PETE GOLDING AND QB TRINIDAD CHAMBLISS TAKE THE TAMPA STAGE
stories.body: First-year Ole Miss coach Pete Golding, who replaced Lane Kiffin after his move to LSU, headlined Wednesday's SEC Media Days session alongside preseason Heisman contender QB Trinidad Chambliss, RB Kewan Lacy, and DT Will Echoles, with Kiffin's own LSU debut and Arch Manning's Texas spotlight still ahead on Thursday.

sports.detail: Jedd Fisch remains in a quiet recruiting stretch while calling plays himself after OC Jimmie Dougherty's departure; 4-star WR commit Tre Moore (Pflugerville, TX) has been drawing buzz at summer 7v7 events. Season opens Sunday, Sept. 6 vs. Washington State (1 p.m. PT, NBC) at Husky Stadium.

Danny Sprinkle remains on hot-seat watch after a 16-17 (7-13 Big Ten) finish; no fresh update on transfer target Boris Tisma or recruit Jaylen Petty this week. Center Hannes Steinbach was picked 14th overall by Charlotte in the 2026 NBA Draft.

Rookies reported to training camp today, first in the league to do so; veterans arrive Friday with nine public practices running July 25-Aug. 13. Seattle signed CB Brandon Johnson to bolster a banged-up secondary, and safety Nick Emmanwori (PUP list, not considered serious) can return anytime. NFL owners vote on the Khosla family's $9.612B purchase Aug. 26.

Restricted free agent center Jalen Duren remains unsigned three-plus weeks into the market, with conflicting reports on whether talks have gained momentum or stalled over a potential 25%-max deal; he could otherwise play 2026-27 on a $9.6M qualifying offer. Detroit finished 60-22 last season (East's No. 1 seed) before falling to Cleveland in the conference semis.

Cincinnati beat Seattle 4-2 Tuesday - Eugenio Suarez homered against his former team and Chase Burns threw 5 scoreless innings, snapping the Mariners' 3-game win streak; Weston Wilson and Julio Rodriguez (15th HR) went deep late but it wasn't enough. Seattle (51-51) hosts the series finale today, 12:40 p.m. PT at T-Mobile Park (Hancock vs. Singer).

deepDive.title: How an Oil Shock Talks to the Fed: Chokepoints, Pass-Through, and the Warsh Put
content: Today's brief has two stories that look separate but aren't: oil jumped 3% to six-week highs on Iran and Houthi escalation, and the same day, prediction markets pushed July rate-hike odds to roughly 26%, climbing toward 43% by September. Those two moves are talking to each other. Central banks don't just watch growth and employment - they watch the inputs that feed directly into the price level, and crude oil is one of the fastest-moving of those inputs. A six-day gap separates today's oil spike from the July 28-29 FOMC meeting, which is exactly enough time for the move to show up in the data the committee sees walking into the room.

The mechanism runs through what's called a chokepoint risk premium. Roughly a fifth of the world's seaborne oil passes through the Strait of Hormuz, and a meaningful share of the rest transits Bab el-Mandeb, the strait Houthi forces are now threatening. Traders don't wait for an actual supply cutoff to reprice crude - they price the probability of one, which is why WTI can jump 3% on strike headlines with zero barrels actually removed from the market. That premium then feeds into CPI through the energy component (historically 6-8% of the headline basket) and indirectly through transport and shipping costs embedded in nearly every other good, typically with a one-to-two-month lag before it shows up in reported inflation.

History is instructive here, and the lesson is that the Fed's response depends entirely on whether the shock looks temporary or structural. After Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, WTI spiked over 30% in weeks, and energy alone added roughly 3 percentage points to that year's headline CPI - yet the Fed ultimately treated most of it as a level shift rather than grounds for permanently higher rates, because a geopolitical supply shock doesn't change the economy's underlying growth capacity the way persistent wage-price spirals do. The 1973-74 oil embargo is the counterexample: that shock arrived on top of already-loose monetary policy and helped entrench a decade of stagflation, precisely because policymakers underestimated how long it would last.

That history is why today's timing matters so much. Warsh's committee already lifted its year-end PCE forecast to 3.6% from 2.7% in June, before this week's oil move - meaning the Fed built in a cushion for exactly this kind of shock, but a six-day-old crude spike heading into the meeting gives hawks a live data point to point to rather than a hypothetical one. Watch the 5-year breakeven inflation rate and the shape of the WTI futures curve over the next few sessions: if breakevens stay anchored and the curve moves into backwardation (near-term prices higher than long-dated ones), markets are pricing this as transitory, the same read the Fed is likely to take. If breakevens drift higher instead, that's the signal a supply shock is starting to look like something the Fed has to lean against with policy, not just acknowledge in a forecast.
